source.title: When is Warmstarting Effective for Scaling Language Models?
source.authors: Neeratyoy Mallik; Maciej Janowski; Johannes Hog; Herilalaina Rakotoarison; Josif Grabocka; Frank Hutter; Aaron Klein

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits validation-loss scaling functions over model parameters and training tokens, a conceptual test of power-law loss scaling in language models, but its main subject is warmstarting rather than reproducing the original scaling-law experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper fits loss surfaces for Scratch, SZP, and Net2Net at approximately 2× growth, and reports fitted coefficients and R² values. It does not prospectively test whether fits on small runs predict much larger runs, nor does it measure a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The downstream benchmark comparison is recorded as related but does not test predictability from scale or pretraining loss. Other cited scaling-law findings are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The scaling-law fits are mainly a tool for locating where warmstarting stops beating Scratch. Still, the study fits the Hoffmann Approach-3 form L(N,D)=E+A/N^α+B/D^β to its own Scratch GPT-2 runs. These are width-only models of 14M–1.2B parameters with µP, a WSD schedule and SlimPajama. It reports fit quality (R²=0.9922), which bears on V1 in a new setting. Fits on warmstarted runs (SZP, Net2Net) bear on whether the form holds in a transfer-style training regime (V5). There is no held-out extrapolation (V2), no compute-optimal allocation estimate (V3), no shape comparison (V4) and no scale-to-downstream relation (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that warmstarting has an upper bound on the growth factor (g_upper) beyond which Scratch is as good, and recommend g=2 as a default. They find gains are largest at or below about 20 tokens/parameter. Their scaling-law fits (all R²>0.99) are used to predict the token budget where warmstarting loses to Scratch, with the caveat that this is subject to fit quality. They make no claim about the original scaling laws themselves.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines model warmstarting and fits loss against parameter count and tokens using the Approach 3 form associated with Hoffmann et al.; it does not reproduce either original study's scaling-law experiment. The fitted comparisons are restricted to approximately 2× growth for the loss-surface analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted exponents differ among Scratch, SZP, and Net2Net. The paper also reports that warmstarting gains vary with growth factor and token budget; its fits use Huber loss (δ=10⁻³) on log loss with L-BFGS-B.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted exponents differ by initialisation method on the LLM runs: α=0.439 for SZP, 0.474 for Net2Net and 0.629 for Scratch; β=0.257, 0.311 and 0.267. The Scratch α is well above Hoffmann's published value, but the paper makes no such comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Warmstarting from a smaller checkpoint changes the fitted parameter and data exponents of the loss law relative to training from scratch.

fits_no_version.finding: At 1.2B parameters, SZP beats Scratch on all six benchmarks (e.g. PIQA 64.6 vs 60.2). This is a single checkpoint per method, with no seeds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SZP warmstarting improves downstream accuracy over Scratch at matched size and budget.

record.problems: The power-law fits are evaluated on the study's collected runs rather than prospectively on much larger held-out runs. The language-model analysis uses a restricted growth-factor subset and the study notes computational limits, unknown base-checkpoint training history, and no multiple seeds or significance testing for the downstream comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant numerical rows were omitted. IsoFLOP growth-factor plots concern warmstarting growth limits rather than the parameter/token/compute laws or compute-optimal parameter-token split specified in the versions.

untested.parts: Compute as a scaling variable. Each variable isolated while the others are non-bottlenecks. Token ranges beyond 10–30 tokens/parameter. Scales beyond 1.2B. Any check other than in-sample R².
All of it: no fit is checked against held-out larger runs.
All of it: there is no compute-optimal N/D allocation estimate. The Chinchilla 20 tokens/parameter line is only drawn as a reference.
All of it: depth is fixed at 8 layers and only width varies.
Image or video models, repeated data and fine-tuning. Only warmstarted LM pretraining and a synthetic MLP regression task are fitted.
All of it: downstream accuracy is reported at one size only.
All of it: there is no comparison of fitting methods, parameter counting or schedules on the same data, and no test of curvature away from a power law.

missing.what: Loss-law fits for the synthetic MLP regression task: Scratch A=1437, α=0.908, B=87, β=0.424, E=0.065, R²=0.9922; SZP R²=0.9994; Net2Net R²=0.9929. These bear on V5 as a non-language setting.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling laws serve as a tool here. The V1 and V5 support rests only on in-sample R² over a narrow token-per-parameter range (10–30), so it is weak evidence. The fits use Huber loss (δ=1e-3) on log L with L-BFGS-B. Figure 4's IsoFLOP curves are over growth factor, not N/D allocation, and do not bear on V3.

versions.untested_parts: The fits use validation loss as a joint function of parameters and tokens for a fixed growth-factor subset. The study does not independently test scaling with compute, isolate each variable while the others are non-bottlenecks, or test the full several-orders-of-magnitude claim across general pretraining setups.
No held-out or prospective test shows that fits from small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study does not estimate how the loss-minimising parameter and token counts scale with a fixed compute budget.
It does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
It does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as settings for the claimed power-law form.
The downstream results compare methods at one model size; they do not test whether task performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.

The paper reports different fitted exponents for Scratch, SZP, and Net2Net, but does not compare fitting methods on the same data, test compute-optimal split sensitivity, or test whether curves bend away from power laws.

rows.subject: GPT-2-style decoder-only language models (SZP)
rows.size_stated: 14M–1.2B parameters overall; fit uses the g≈2 subset
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss as a function of parameters N and training tokens D
rows.measure: Fitted loss function: L(N,D)=E+A/N^α+B/D^β; fit quality R²
rows.note: A fitted scaling relationship on the study's collected runs, not a prospective prediction test.
rows.check: This is a warmstarted (SZP-initialised) training regime, not plain pretraining from scratch, so it belongs to V5 (transfer-style regime) rather than V1. Its V7 link is removed: different exponents across initialisation methods describe different training procedures, not fitting or setup dependence of one law. The study does not frame it as V7 either.

rows.subject: GPT-2-style decoder-only language models (Scratch)
rows.size_stated: 14M–1.2B parameters overall; fit uses the g≈2 subset
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss as a function of parameters N and training tokens D
rows.measure: Fitted loss function: L(N,D)=E+A/N^α+B/D^β; fit quality R²
rows.note: The paper says all reported R² values exceed 0.99.
rows.check: This is a Scratch fit, so 'g=1' rather than the g≈2 subset. R²=0.9922 is the only quality measure; there are no residuals and no held-out check. The token range is narrow (10–30 tokens/parameter), so the D term is weakly identified. The V7 link is removed: the paper does not compare its exponents (α=0.629) with published laws or test fitting choices.

relation.reason: Reports fitted loss functions and their R² values, providing evidence on the claimed power-law form beyond using it to predict warmstarting crossovers.

tranche.reason: Reports scaling-law fit quality in a new warmstarting setting, including a controlled Scratch comparison; its own results bear on V1 and V5.

source_check.notes: The reported R² values measure in-sample fit; no held-out extrapolation check or fit uncertainty is reported. The tested range does not independently establish V1's non-bottleneck conditions or behavior over several orders of magnitude.
